content:
At a rally in Texas for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, President Donald Trump was interrupted by protesters more than ten times, after which he insulted them on stage.

"That guy needs to lose some weight," Trump said as one protester was being escorted out.

Speaking of another protester, he said: "He's going home to find his mom... but what he doesn't know is that his mom voted for Trump."

The president also baselessly claimed that the protesters were paid to boo. "These are paid protesters, bought by our country's enemies," Trump said without any evidence.

As he uttered these words and watched the protesters move through the crowd, his body language and facial expressions gave him away.

Clinical psychologist and behaviour expert Denise Dudley said: "In this scenario, we have to remember one thing — he's in his element. This isn't a cross-party thing... he's with his people. So his approach isn't simply to eject them, but to make the most of the opportunity."

Dudley added that he employed a technique called "audience-facing reframing," saying "he turned the protesters' interruptions into an opportunity to define the event more clearly for his supporters."

She pointed out that Trump created an "in-group/out-group" moment, a tactic people use to distinguish supporters from critics, even "good people" from "bad people."

Trump repeatedly commented on the motives and appearance of his opponents.

Dudley said: "He described the out-group to the in-group, which got the in-group even more fired up... they started chanting 'USA,' so he used this very effectively — essentially saying: 'Look at us over here, and look at those horrible people over there. They're paid protesters.'"

She added: "He's basically attacking them to make his own camp more united. So this is a strategy."

Experts noted that Trump makes tongue movements at certain moments, which signal frustration.

Body language expert Patti Wood, author of "Snap: Making the Most of First Impressions, Body Language, and Charisma," said that throughout the rally, Trump made tongue movements multiple times, which speaks volumes.

At one point, "he pressed his tongue against the inside of his cheek and pushed outward — this is a gesture of frustration."

Wood said: "He also made what's called a 'tongue-out gesture' during a moment of frustration, sticking his tongue out."

She said: "This is one of my favourite non-verbal behaviours to spot in people in high positions of power, because it mirrors playground behaviour — when a bully is picking on a kid who can't fight back on the playground, they'll stick their tongue out."

She noted that the gesture was quick but a "very instinctive" response.

Wood said: "This is a tell-tale sign of his frustration, and he does it just before launching an attack."

Wood said: "I see this gesture often during suspect transports... generally, in any context, you wouldn't expect to see this reaction in a president, because they hold the power," she said, "so this tells me that on some level, he feels he doesn't hold the power — and that's a rather telling revelation."

His clenched jaw and tight-lipped movements showed he was suppressing tension.

Behavioural scientist Abbie Maroño said: "When you look at his face, you can't miss his lips."

Trump's mouth and lips moved a great deal as he spoke and interacted.

Maroño said Trump "often presses his lips together when he's agitated. So his baseline already involves a lot of lip movement, but this time it was really exaggerated."

She said it's interesting that this movement appears every time he tries to reframe the protesters' interruptions positively.

Maroño said: "He displays very extreme lip-pressing. Now, lip-pressing is a behaviour we use to almost not verbalise a certain piece of information... it's a display of restraint, something we do when we're trying to hold back, feeling annoyed, or embarrassed and wanting to say something."

Wood added that lip-pressing can carry multiple meanings, but usually signals disgust.

Maroño noted that his jaw was also visibly clenched. "You can see how tight and pronounced it is... his jaw isn't just clenched, it repeatedly juts forward."

Maroño said this shows he was trying to suppress "extreme" agitation and frustration.

He would stop and stare at some protesters as they were being removed, which experts said was a "selfish move."

As some protesters were being escorted out of the venue, Trump deliberately paused his remarks and stared at them as they were led away. This made everyone present stop and watch as well.

Dudley said that whether you were an audience member in the room or watching the rally broadcast on TV, "nothing happens until those protesters are removed."

Dudley said: "He just stops and stares — this forces all of us to know the protesters are being removed. Even if we can't see, we know exactly what's happening." In a sense, this is making an example of someone.

Dudley said: "I think this part could be called the most selfish move." She added that people came to the rally to hear Trump speak, but he stopped the entire performance to stare and wait for the outcome.

She said this was his way of bringing the whole rally to a halt so that everyone could watch the "naughty protesters" being led out of the room.

Certain head movements and mouth expressions showed that Trump was feeling "frustrated" and "exhausted" by the interruptions.

Maroño said: "I noticed several times he would lift his chin, and that's something we do when we feel proud or are trying to project confidence."

She pointed out that this is why people remind themselves to keep their heads up when trying to appear confident.

She said: "There were several times he kept lifting his head, so he was trying to project confidence." But Maroño added that combined with his hidden frustration, this created a vibe of "combative confidence."

She said: "He wasn't calm and composed. He's putting on a front, but he's agitated inside."

With more than 12 protester interruptions that evening, it's no wonder Trump felt frustrated — though he didn't want the protesters to see that their actions were working.

Maroño said: "The election is very close now, it's like a long war where you once had so much drive, motivation and passion, but as you near the end, like a final sprint, you're already exhausted."

She added: "In his recent appearances, I've started seeing more clearly that he seems somewhat agitated."

Wood agreed, noting that after Trump's remark about "these are paid protesters," his eyes would "flicker" and his mouth formed a downward arc.

Wood said: "This tells me... he's exhausted." She added: "That statement didn't carry force, and afterwards he was worn out by the thought that those people were actually in the audience."

Wood said Trump's supporters also booed the protesters, which she believes confused Trump.

Wood said: "For a moment I was wondering, was he thinking: 'Are those boos for me?' Like what happened to him at a football game." Trump was booed by the crowd at a Washington Commanders game last year.

Wood said: "I think this shows that the negative remarks from those people affected him."

Wood added that the pauses before responding to or acknowledging what was happening also showed he needed time to figure out what he actually wanted to do or say.

His instinct is to attack immediately, ignore, or cut someone off, but "he didn't do that this time."

Wood said: "In terms of immediately launching an attack, he wasn't his usual self."
